title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

learn.hook: Will it rain on Sports Day? Will India win the toss? Life is full of 'maybe', and maths can measure it!
points: Probability measures how likely an event is: how confident we can be that it will happen.
Uncertain situations are everywhere: rain tomorrow, the result of a match, whose name is drawn from a box of slips.
In words we say an event is impossible, less likely, equally likely (even chance), more likely or certain.
Subjective probability is a personal judgement. Two fans may give different chances to the same team winning, based on their feelings and knowledge.

example.q: Describe each in words: (a) the Sun rises tomorrow, (b) a fair coin shows heads, (c) you roll a 7 on an ordinary die.
steps: (b) Heads and tails have the same chance: equally likely
(c) A die has only 1 to 6: impossible

learn.reallife: Weather reports say '70% chance of rain', turning 'maybe' into a number you can plan with.

How many people like an event

quiz.q: Which event is certain?

You draw a red card from a full deck

steps: An ordinary die has faces 1 to 6 only.

quiz.q: A box has 5 slips with your friends' names, one each. One slip is drawn. The chance that a particular friend's name comes is:

quiz.q: Meena says there is a 90% chance her school team will win; Arjun says 60%. What kind of probability are they using?

steps: 90% and 60% are personal judgements of the same match.
They are not from data or equally likely outcomes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any percentage is objective

quiz.q: A bag has 9 green balls and 1 yellow ball. Getting a yellow ball is:
quiz.explain: Only 1 of 10 balls is yellow.
steps: Only 1 of the 10 balls is yellow.
It is possible, but not likely.

quiz.q: A bag has 9 green balls and 1 yellow ball. Getting a green ball is:
quiz.explain: 9 of the 10 balls are green.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What does it mean when we say something is 'likely'?"

revise.summary: Probability measures how likely an event is. In words, events are impossible, less likely, equally likely, more likely or certain. Subjective probability is a personal judgement.
remember: Sun rises tomorrow: certain. Fair coin heads: equally likely. 7 on a die: impossible.
9 green and 1 yellow: yellow less likely, green more likely.
Subjective = personal judgement, can differ between people.
traps: 'Very likely' is not 'certain'.
'Unlikely' is not 'impossible'.

learn.hook: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. Heads or tails? Nobody knows for sure, but maths can still say how likely each one is!
points: A random experiment is an action whose result cannot be predicted for certain, like tossing a coin or rolling a die.
Each possible result is an outcome. The list of all outcomes is the sample space: rolling a die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a collection of outcomes, such as 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
When all outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 to 1. A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0.

example.q: A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.

learn.reallife: Ludo, snakes and ladders and the cricket toss are all random experiments. Fair dice and coins make the game fair for everyone.

quiz.q: Which event is impossible?
options: Getting an odd number on a die
Getting a head on a coin
Getting a number less than 3 on a die
quiz.explain: A normal die only has 1 to 6, so 7 can never come up. Its probability is 0.
steps: A normal die shows only 1 to 6.
7 can never come up, so P = 0.

quiz.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?

quiz.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls of the same size. One ball is picked without looking. What is P(red)?
quiz.explain: There are 3 + 5 = 8 equally likely balls, and 3 of them are red. P(red) = 3/8.

quiz.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts coloured red, blue, green and yellow. What is the probability that it does NOT stop on red?
quiz.explain: Three of the four equal parts are not red, so P(not red) = 3/4.

quiz.q: A die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the event 'getting a prime number'?
quiz.explain: The primes from 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5. The number 1 is not prime.
steps: 1 is not prime; 4 and 6 are composite.
quiz.mistake: Counts 1 as a prime number, getting 4

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Of the 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, two (HT and TH) have exactly one head. P = 2/4 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks there are only 3 outcomes, so gives 1/3

teach.ask: Gappu holds a die: "What does it mean to say the chance of rolling a 6 is 1/6?"
teach.praise: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only 1 of them is a 6, so the chance is 1 out of 6. Now I understand dice!
teach.nudge: How many different results can the die show, and are they all equally likely?

revise.summary: A random experiment has outcomes; all outcomes form the sample space, and an event is a set of outcomes. For equally likely outcomes, P = favourable ÷ total, between 0 and 1.
traps: Probability cannot be more than 1.
1 is not a prime number.
Divide by the total, not by the other outcomes.

learn.hook: Every chance in the world fits on one ruler from 0 to 1!
points: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). 0 means impossible, 1 means certain.
An even chance, like heads on a fair coin, is 0.5 or 50%.
Events can be ranked on the scale: less likely events sit nearer 0, more likely ones nearer 1. Always give a reason.
A fair (unbiased) coin, die or spinner makes every outcome equally likely; a bent coin or loaded die is biased.

example.q: Place on the 0-1 scale: (a) a fair die shows 6, (b) a fair coin shows heads, (c) it is cold in Delhi in January.

learn.reallife: Sports commentators say a team has a '50-50 chance'—that's 0.5 on the probability scale.

learn.hook: Toss a paper cup: does it land on its side, top or bottom? Opinions won't help. Experiments will!
points: Objective probability is based on evidence or reasoning, not opinion.
Two objective ways: from experiments or observations (experimental), and from reasoning about equally likely outcomes (theoretical).
Frequency is how many times an outcome happened; relative frequency is frequency ÷ total trials, which is the experimental probability.
To run trials: fix the experiment, repeat it many times, record each result with tally marks, then count frequencies.
For objects like a paper cup, outcomes are not equally likely, so only experiments can estimate the probabilities.

example.q: A paper cup is tossed 50 times: side 31, top 12, bottom 7. Find the relative frequencies.

learn.reallife: Cricket statisticians use relative frequencies, like a batter's fraction of innings with fifties.

teach.praise: Exactly! Frequency counts, relative frequency divides by the total number of trials!

revise.summary: Objective probability comes from experiments or from reasoning about equally likely outcomes. Relative frequency = frequency ÷ total trials.
remember: Cup in 50 tosses: side 0.62, top 0.24, bottom 0.14 (sum 1).
Tally: four lines and a cross line = 5.
traps: Frequency is a count; relative frequency is a proportion.
A paper cup's outcomes are not equally likely.

learn.hook: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the share of heads creeps very close to one half. Let's see why!
points: Experimental (empirical) probability is found by actually doing an experiment many times.
P(E) = number of trials in which E happened ÷ total number of trials.
Different runs of the same experiment can give slightly different results.
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.
The experimental probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

example.q: Kabir tosses a coin 50 times and gets 28 heads. Find the experimental probability of heads and of tails.

learn.reallife: Weather offices say there is a 70% chance of rain because, on past days with similar conditions, it rained on about 70 out of 100 of them.

items.q: 36 of 120 students walk to school: P(walks)?

games.title: What do experiments tell us?
items: If you repeat an experiment, you always get exactly the same probability
Random results change from run to run, so the experimental probability can change too.
More trials usually give an experimental probability closer to the theoretical value
Over many trials the lucky and unlucky runs balance out.
An experimental probability of 0.4 means the event happened in 40% of the trials
Getting 7 heads in 10 tosses proves the coin is unfair
With so few tosses, 7 heads can happen by chance with a fair coin.
Experimental probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1
Every trial gives exactly one outcome, so the counts add up to the total number of trials.

quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical value 0.5 instead of the data

quiz.q: A die is rolled 60 times and a 6 appears 12 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 6?
quiz.explain: P(6) = 12 ÷ 60 = 1/5. The theoretical value 1/6 is close but not the same.
steps: (Theoretical 1/6 is close but not the same.)
quiz.mistake: Writes the theoretical probability 1/6 instead of using the experiment's data

quiz.q: In a survey of 40 students, 14 said cricket is their favourite sport. What is the probability that a student picked at random from them likes cricket most?

quiz.mistake: Divides 25 by 5, or reads 5 as 0.5

quiz.q: A shop checks 500 bulbs and finds 20 defective. What is the probability that a bulb picked at random is NOT defective?
quiz.explain: Good bulbs = 500 − 20 = 480, so P(not defective) = 480 ÷ 500 = 0.96.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(defective) = 0.04 instead

quiz.q: Aisha rolled a die 30 times: 1 came 4 times, 2 came 6 times, 3 came 5 times, 4 came 3 times, 5 came 7 times and 6 came 5 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 5?
quiz.explain: 5 came 7 times out of 30 rolls, so P(5) = 7/30.
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical 1/6, or divides by the other rolls (23)

quiz.q: Which statement about experimental probability is true?
options: It is always exactly equal to the theoretical probability
It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.explain: It comes from actual results, which vary from one run of trials to the next.
steps: Experimental probability comes from actual results.
Results vary from one run of trials to another.
It cannot exceed 1 and needs data.
Answer: It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.mistake: Thinks experimental and theoretical probability are always the same

quiz.q: From past records, the experimental probability of rain on a July day in a town is 0.35. What is the probability of no rain?

teach.ask: Gappu tossed a coin 10 times and got 7 heads: "So is the chance of heads 7/10 now? I thought it was 1/2!"
teach.praise: 7/10 is the experimental probability from your 10 trials. With many more tosses it should get closer to 1/2. Clever!
teach.nudge: How did you get 7/10? And what might happen if you tossed the coin 1000 times?

revise.summary: Experimental probability = trials where E happened ÷ total trials. It varies between runs and usually gets closer to the theoretical probability as trials grow.
traps: Use the data, not the theoretical 1/6 or 0.5.
Divide by the total trials.
Experimental and theoretical values are not always equal.

learn.hook: A factory cannot test every single pen it makes. So how does it know how many might be faulty? Probability makes the prediction!
points: Expected number of times an event happens = probability × number of trials.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E), because an event either happens or does not.
The probabilities of all the outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
A prediction is a good estimate, not a promise: the real count may be a little more or less.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

example.q: A factory found 3 faulty pens in a sample of 150. About how many faulty pens should it expect in a batch of 2000?

learn.reallife: Insurance companies, doctors and weather forecasters all use probability from past data to plan for the future.

quiz.q: In a game with one die, Riya wins if it shows 6 and Arjun wins if it shows 1 to 5. Is the game fair?
options: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6
Yes, because a die is fair

steps: Unequal chances, so the game is not fair.
Answer: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6

quiz.q: Arjun tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. What can he conclude?

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "If the chance of rain is 0.3, how many rainy days should I expect in 30 days? And is it guaranteed?"
teach.praise: Multiply 0.3 by 30 to expect about 9 rainy days, but it is an estimate, not a promise. I'll carry an umbrella anyway!
teach.nudge: How do you turn a probability into an expected number? Is the prediction certain?

revise.summary: Expected number = probability × number of trials. Probabilities of all outcomes add to 1. A game is fair when every player has the same chance.
focus: Decide if a game is fair.
remember: Expected = P × trials; 3 faulty in 150 → 40 in 2000.
Fair game: equal chances for all players.
traps: P(not E) is not the reciprocal of P(E).
A fair die does not make every game fair.
Short runs prove nothing; coins don't remember.

topics.title: Many trials, fair outcomes and the gambler's fallacy

learn.hook: Five heads in a row: is tails 'due' now? Nope! The coin has no memory!
points: Law of large numbers: with more and more trials, the experimental probability tends to get closer to the theoretical one.
Rolling a fair die 60 times may give 6 about 10 times, but maybe 7 or 14; in 6000 rolls the relative frequency is usually very close to 1/6.
Gambler's fallacy: believing that past results change future chances. Each toss of a fair coin is still 1/2 heads, even after 5 heads in a row.
Before using 'favourable ÷ total', check the outcomes are equally likely. 'Win, lose or draw' are three outcomes, but they are usually not equally likely, so P(win) is not automatically 1/3.

example.q: A fair die is rolled 600 times and shows 6 on 94 rolls. Compare experimental and theoretical probability.
steps: Close, and likely to get closer with more rolls

learn.reallife: Lottery players sometimes pick 'overdue' numbers, but every draw is a fresh start. That's the gambler's fallacy.

quiz.mistake: Believes tails is 'due' (gambler's fallacy)

quiz.q: Which is an example of the gambler's fallacy?
options: 'A fair die gives each number with chance 1/6'
'Number 3 hasn't come in 20 rolls, so it's due next'
'The coin is fair, so heads is 1/2'
quiz.explain: Past results do not make a number 'due'.
steps: Gambler's fallacy: thinking past results change future chances.
'3 is due' assumes a gap makes 3 more likely.
Answer: 'Number 3 hasn't come in 20 rolls, so it's due next'
quiz.mistake: Thinks long gaps change chances

quiz.q: Riya rolls a fair die 60 times and gets 6 on 15 rolls. Which is most reasonable?
options: Random variation; with thousands of rolls it would likely settle near 1/6
quiz.explain: 60 rolls is a small sample; 15 is possible by chance.
steps: Expected 6s in 60 rolls ≈ 10; 15 is possible by chance.
With thousands of rolls the relative frequency tends to 1/6.
Answer: Random variation; with thousands of rolls it would likely settle near 1/6
quiz.mistake: Draws strong conclusions from a small sample

quiz.q: A die is rolled 6000 times. About how many times should 2 appear?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 6

quiz.q: Which experiment's relative frequency is most likely to be close to the theoretical probability?
quiz.explain: More trials generally give results closer to the theory.
steps: Law of large numbers: more trials → closer to theory.
6000 is the largest number of trials.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer trials are more accurate

quiz.q: A football match can end in win, loss or draw for India. Why is P(win) not simply 1/3?
options: The three outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.explain: The formula needs equally likely outcomes; team strength changes the chances.
steps: Favourable ÷ total needs equally likely outcomes.
Win, loss and draw depend on team strength.
So they are not equally likely.
Answer: The three outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.mistake: Applies favourable ÷ total without checking equal likelihood

quiz.q: A spinner has sectors of 180°, 90° and 90° coloured red, blue and green. Are the colours equally likely?
options: No; red has probability 1/2, blue and green 1/4 each
Yes, because there are three colours
quiz.explain: Chance depends on the size of each sector, not the number of colours.
steps: Answer: No; red has probability 1/2, blue and green 1/4 each
quiz.mistake: Counts colours instead of comparing sector sizes

quiz.q: For a fair die, which pair of events is equally likely?
options: Getting a 6 and getting less than 6
Getting an odd number and getting an even number
quiz.explain: Odd {1, 3, 5} and even {2, 4, 6} each have 3 outcomes.
steps: The other pairs have 1 vs 5 or 3 vs 1 outcomes.
Answer: Getting an odd number and getting an even number
quiz.mistake: Thinks single numbers and groups are equally likely

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "After 5 heads in a row, isn't tails more likely now?"
teach.praise: Right! The coin has no memory; it's still 1/2 each time!
teach.nudge: Does the coin remember what happened before? What is the chance on every toss?

revise.summary: With more trials, experimental probability tends towards the theoretical value. Past results never change the chance of a fair coin or die. Favourable ÷ total needs equally likely outcomes.
focus: Explain the law of large numbers.
Check equal likelihood before using the formula.
traps: No outcome is ever 'due'.
Win, lose, draw are not automatically 1/3 each.
Count sector sizes, not colours.

learn.hook: A coin and a die together: how many different results? A tree diagram grows the answer branch by branch!
points: List the sample space carefully: one coin {H, T}; one die {1, ..., 6}; two coins {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
A coin with a die gives 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes: H1, H2, ..., T6. Two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes.
Menus and choices: 3 snacks and 2 drinks give 3 × 2 = 6 combinations.
A tree diagram shows multi-step experiments: each stage branches into its outcomes; the number of end branches is the size of the sample space.

example.q: Draw a tree for tossing a coin three times. How many outcomes, and what is P(exactly two heads)?

learn.reallife: A canteen offering 4 types of paratha and 3 chutneys can advertise 12 different combos!

quiz.q: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
quiz.explain: 2 outcomes × 6 outcomes.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 + 6

quiz.q: For a coin and a die together, what is P(tails and a number greater than 4)?
quiz.explain: T5 and T6: 2 favourable out of 12 = 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of T5, T6

quiz.q: Two dice are rolled. How many ways can the sum be 8?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that (2,6) and (6,2) are different

quiz.q: Two dice are rolled. What is P(sum = 8)?
quiz.explain: 5 favourable outcomes out of 36.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 11 possible sums as equally likely

quiz.q: A thali has a choice of 3 sabzis, 2 dals and 2 sweets. How many different thalis can be made?
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices

quiz.q: Three coins are tossed. What is P(at least one tail)?
quiz.explain: Only HHH has no tail: 1 − 1/8.
steps: No tail only in HHH: 1 outcome.
quiz.mistake: Counts 'exactly one tail'

quiz.q: In a tree diagram for two tosses of a coin, how many end branches are there?
quiz.explain: Each first branch splits into two: 2 × 2.
steps: Each splits into 2 for the second toss: 2 × 2 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks HT and TH are the same

quiz.q: Kavya chooses a uniform: 2 shirts (white, blue) and 3 trousers (grey, black, navy). What is P(white shirt with black trousers) if she picks at random?
quiz.explain: One combination out of 2 × 3 = 6.
steps: White with black is 1 of them.
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices to get 5

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I list all outcomes when tossing a coin and rolling a die?"
teach.praise: Excellent! A tree or table shows 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes!
teach.nudge: How can you organise the outcomes? How many does each stage add?

revise.summary: List sample spaces carefully: a coin and a die give 12 outcomes, two dice give 36. Choices multiply, and tree diagrams show multi-step experiments.
focus: Find probabilities with two dice or three coins.
remember: Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Three coins: 8 outcomes; exactly two heads 3/8.
traps: HT and TH are different outcomes.
Multiply the choices; don't add them.
The 11 sums of two dice are not equally likely.

learn.hook: Put the sweet back or eat it? The answer changes your next chance!
points: With replacement, the object goes back, so the sample space is the same for every draw. Without replacement, it shrinks by one each draw.
Example: a bag of 3 red and 2 blue. Ordered draws of two: with replacement 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes; without replacement 5 × 4 = 20.
From a frequency table, P(outcome) = its frequency ÷ total. For spinners, use the fraction of the circle (angle ÷ 360°). For letter cards, count the letters.
Geometric probability: if a dart lands at a random point of a board, P(region) = area of region ÷ area of board.

example.q: A dart lands randomly on a square board of side 20 cm with a square target of side 10 cm in the middle. Find P(target).

learn.reallife: Lucky-draw organisers at a school fete decide whether to put tickets back after each draw: it changes everyone's chances.

Bag 3R 2B, without replacement: P(R then R)

quiz.q: A bag has 4 red and 1 green ball. A ball is drawn and NOT put back, then a second is drawn. How many ordered outcomes are there?
quiz.explain: 5 choices for the first and 4 for the second: 5 × 4.
steps: Without replacement: 5 choices for the first draw.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 × 5 as if the ball were replaced

quiz.q: Same bag (4 red, 1 green), drawing two without replacement. What is P(both red)?
quiz.explain: Favourable ordered pairs: 4 × 3 = 12 out of 20.
steps: Both red: 4 choices first, then 3 red left: 4 × 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Uses with-replacement counting

quiz.q: Same bag, drawing two WITH replacement. What is P(both red)?
quiz.explain: 4 × 4 = 16 favourable out of 5 × 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Reduces the count as if without replacement

quiz.q: A survey of 50 families: 0 cars 12, 1 car 26, 2 cars 9, 3 or more 3. What is P(a family has exactly 1 car)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 100

quiz.q: The letters of the word MATHEMATICS are on 11 cards. One card is drawn. What is P(M)?
quiz.explain: M appears twice among 11 letters.
quiz.mistake: Counts M only once

quiz.q: A spinner has a blue sector of 135°. What is P(blue)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 180

quiz.q: A dartboard is a circle of radius 10 cm with a bullseye of radius 2 cm. A dart hits the board at random. What is P(bullseye)?
quiz.mistake: Compares radii instead of areas

quiz.q: A rectangular field 40 m × 25 m has a pond of area 100 m². A seed falls at a random spot. What is P(it falls in the pond)?
quiz.explain: Field area 1000 m²; 100 ÷ 1000.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Does putting the ball back change the probability of the second draw?"
teach.praise: Yes! With replacement the bag stays the same; without it, the bag shrinks!
teach.nudge: How many balls are there for the second draw if you don't put the first back?

revise.summary: With replacement the sample space stays the same; without replacement it shrinks. Use frequency tables, spinner angles or areas to find probabilities.
focus: Count draws with and without replacement.
Find probabilities from tables, letters and spinners.
remember: 3 red, 2 blue: with replacement 25 ordered outcomes; without 20.
Dartboard: P = region area ÷ board area; 400 board, 100 target → 1/4.
traps: Don't reduce the count when the ball is replaced.
Compare areas, not radii.
Count repeated letters each time.
